newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Labour Party plan for tobacco ad ban lights up debate.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Labour Party plan for tobacco ad ban lights up debate.

text.p: Britain's Labour Party, widely tipped to win the May 1 election, promises to ban all tobacco advertising, the final blow after more than 30 years of increasing restrictions.

Manufacturers and advertisers say a ban would hurt industry without improving anyone's health, but appear resigned that Labour, if elected, will honour the promise contained in its election manifesto.

"It's quite clear that there is a link between advertising and smoking," Kevin Barron, Labour's public health spokesman, told Reuters in a telephone interview. "It is one of the reasons why young people pick up the habit."
The tobacco and advertising industries contend that cigarette advertising merely influences the brand choice of existing smokers.

"They think they will reduce consumption overall, because that is their objective," Clive Turner, executive director of industry affairs for Britain's Tobacco Manufacturers Association (TMA), told Reuters. "We would say there's no real evidence from around the world that that is so...

"If there were a ban we would be robbed of the ability to compete with one another," Turner said. "We've got about 300 brands on sale here...about 30 percent of smokers during a given year tend to switch brands and many more tend to smoke more than one brand."
Turner said the TMA is not acting aggressively to oppose a ban. "We are trying to persuade thoughtful members of parliament to listen to what we say," he said.
Smoking reached its peak in Britain in the early 1970s with annual sales of 140 billion cigarettes. Consumption is now about 85 billion cigarettes, according to the TMA.
Tobacco manufacturers say they spend about 50 million pounds ($81.4 million) a year on advertising in Britain, including about eight million for sponsorship deals.
DECLINE IN ADVERTISING SINCE TV ADS BANNED
Tobacco advertising spending peaked in the early 1960s at 140 million pounds before dropping sharply in the mid-1960s when television advertising was banned.

Tobacco advertising has since been banned on radio and is severely restricted in other media. Advertisements may be carried in newspapers and magazines, in cinemas, and on billboards. They are banned from bus shelters and on buses themselves.
TMA's Turner said the decline in advertising spending over the last 30 years reflected the growing restrictions. "We've got lots of avenues closed to us now," he said.

Barron said he could not say how long it would take Labour to implement a ban. "Any legislation would be competing for parliamentary time with other pieces of legislation," he said. "But we would like it to be done as soon as possible."
Tobacco companies would still be allowed to sponsor sporting events, Barron said.
WHO WOULD BE AFFECTED BY A BAN?
It is not clear who would be affected by an advertising ad ban.
An advertising trade group said a ban would deal a symbolic blow against the advertising industry rather than a serious monetary blow.

"In volume it's not a huge sector," Lionel Stanbrook, deputy director-general of Britain's Advertising Association, a federation of 27 trade and professional groups, told Reuters. "It would be a blow because it's a symbolic issue...

"We think it breaks the principle of the freedom to advertise anything that's legally sold," Stanbrook added. "You can't get away from the fact that millions of people go and buy it everyday. You're not going to solve that problem by banning advertising."
While outdoor advertising is a key medium for the tobacco industry, major players said they felt a ban would not necessarily inflict severe pain.

"If it's banned overnight then it's obviously very dramatic," Francis Goodwin, managing director of Maiden Outdoor, the billboard division of outdoor advertisesr Maiden Group Plc. "If it's a phased-in period, then (the impact) could take years."

Tobacco is already a declining segment of Maiden's business, accounting for 8.4 percent of revenues in 1996 and expected to fall to five percent in 1997, the company said. More O'Ferrall Plc, Britain's largest outdoor advertiser, said tobacco accounts for only one percent of its business.
Goodwin did say that any ban would pressure selling rates of outdoor advertising companies because a ban would reduce overall demand for billboards.

But while about 20 million pounds a year of tobacco advertising is spent on outdoor ads -- close to half of the tobacco industry's adspend -- it represents only a small proportion of the outdoor advertising industry. "We're talking about a 420 million pound market," said Goodwin.

The Advertising Association's Stanbrook said magazines would suffer most under a tobacco ad ban."It will cut the revenue of the independent media," he said. "Some magazines rely quite heavily on tobacco advertising," he added, noting that he would expect some magazines to fold.
HEALTH ISSUE CONTENTIOUS
The health issue, meanwhile, remains highly contentious.

One brochure from the tobacco industry notes that a 1990 government report on "Why Children Start Smoking" cited seven reasons on why children smoke, but mentions that they do not include advertising.

Labour's Barron, however, said that one of the stated reasons for smoking -- "having relatively less negative views about smoking" -- is a clear sign that advertising does encourage children to take up smoking.
"How do you get positive and negative views in society?" he said. "It is promoted (in ads) as glamorous."
Moreover, he added, over 70 percent of current smokers start smoking between the ages of 11 to 15. The legal age for buying tobacco in Britain is 16.
The Labour Party has said the primary purpose of an advertising ban is to discourage young people from smoking.
Existing regulations prohibit tobacco ads aimed at children, including a ban on advertisements in publications targeted at children.

A recent study by the MVA Consultancy, however, found that children are influenced by cigarette ads. "The Voluntary Code on Tobacco Advertising between the United Kingdom Health Departments and the tobacco industry is not effective in protecting children from the impact of cigarette advertisements," it said. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
